lectures.title: Vectors
lectures.summary: How to represent, add and multiply vectors, which is the language every later topic uses.
outcomes: Represent, add and subtract vectors graphically.
Resolve vectors into components and reconstruct their magnitude and direction.
Add vectors using components and unit-vector notation.
Calculate and interpret dot and cross products.

lectures.title: Motion
lectures.summary: How position, velocity and acceleration describe motion, from free fall to projectiles and circles.
outcomes: Describe motion using position, displacement, velocity and acceleration.
Interpret motion using diagrams, graphs and equations.
Select and apply appropriate kinematic models.
Apply kinematics to free fall, projectile, circular and relative motion.

lectures.title: Newton's laws
lectures.summary: How forces are drawn in free-body diagrams and how they determine acceleration.
outcomes: Identify forces and represent them using free-body diagrams.
Apply Newton's laws to equilibrium and accelerating systems.
Model normal force, tension and friction in physical systems.
Solve connected-object, inclined-plane and circular-dynamics problems.

lectures.title: Work and kinetic energy
lectures.summary: When a force does work, and how that work changes the speed of an object.
outcomes: Calculate the work done by a constant force, and the total work done on an object.
Interpret the sign of work and the meaning of kinetic energy.
Apply the work–energy theorem to find speeds, distances and forces.
Calculate the work done by varying forces, including springs, and relate work to power.

lectures.title: Potential energy and energy conservation
lectures.summary: How stored energy and conservation of energy solve problems that forces alone make difficult.
outcomes: Calculate gravitational and elastic potential energy, and say when a force has a potential energy.
Apply conservation of mechanical energy to find speeds and heights.
Include friction and other forces in an energy equation, and say where the energy goes.
Find a force from a potential energy, and read an energy diagram.

lectures.title: Impulse and momentum
lectures.summary: How impulse changes momentum, and how conservation of momentum solves collision problems.
outcomes: Calculate momentum and impulse, and relate them with the impulse–momentum theorem.
Apply conservation of momentum to isolated systems.
Solve one- and two-dimensional collision problems, and classify collisions as elastic or inelastic.
Use the coefficient of restitution and combine collisions with energy methods.

lectures.title: Rotation
lectures.summary: How torque, moment of inertia and angular momentum extend Newton's laws to rotating bodies.
outcomes: Describe rotation using angular position, velocity and acceleration, and relate them to the linear motion of a point on the body.
Calculate moments of inertia and torques, and use Στ = Iα to find angular accelerations.
Use work, power and energy methods for rotating and rolling bodies.
Use angular momentum and its conservation, including when the moment of inertia changes.

lectures.title: Temperature and heat
lectures.summary: What temperature and heat mean, how they are measured, and how heat moves between bodies.
outcomes: Distinguish temperature from heat, and explain thermal equilibrium and the zeroth law.
Convert between the Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales and describe how thermometers work.
Calculate thermal expansion and the heat needed to change a temperature, including simple calorimetry.
Calculate the rate of heat transfer by conduction and radiation, and describe convection.

lectures.title: Thermal properties of matter
lectures.summary: How the ideal-gas equation, phase changes and kinetic theory describe matter at the molecular level.
outcomes: Use the ideal-gas equation and the gas laws to calculate and compare the states of a gas.
Read pV and phase diagrams, and calculate the heat in a phase change, including calorimetry.
State the assumptions of the kinetic theory and explain pressure and temperature in terms of molecular motion.
Calculate the average kinetic energy and the rms speed of molecules, and select the right model in an unfamiliar problem.

lectures.title: First law of thermodynamics
lectures.summary: How energy is exchanged as heat and work, and how the first law describes each gas process.
outcomes: Describe a thermodynamic system, state and process, and calculate the work done by a gas from a pV diagram.
Apply the first law, ΔU = Q − W, to a process and to a cycle.
Calculate Q, W and ΔU for isochoric, isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes of an ideal gas.
Analyse a multi-step process or cycle in an unfamiliar problem, choosing the physics without being told.

lectures.title: Second law of thermodynamics
lectures.summary: Why processes run in one direction, what entropy measures, and the best efficiency an engine can reach.
outcomes: Distinguish reversible from irreversible processes, and calculate entropy changes to decide whether a process is allowed.
Analyse a heat engine or a refrigerator with an energy-flow diagram, including from a pV cycle.
State the second law and use the Carnot cycle to find the maximum efficiency and to test a claimed device.
Analyse an unfamiliar engine, refrigerator or entropy problem, choosing the physics without being told.
